Hon. C. J. DOHERTY moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 39, to amend the Canadian Patriotic Fund Act, 1914. He said:
This Bill is intended to amend the

Act for two purposes:	first, to enable
the Corporation created by the Act of 1914 to assist the wives, children and dependent relatives of residents of Newfoundland who may be on active service during the present war in the military or naval forces of Canada; secondly, to assist men of the Canadian expeditionary forces who may become incapacitated in the course of the war and return to Canada; and likewise to assist the widows and dependent relatives of members of the Canadian expeditionary forces who may be killed during the war. Under the present Act, the power to extend assistance to wives, children and dependent relatives is limited to relatives of residents of Canada actually serving in the expeditionary forces; so that under the law as it now stands, assistance could not be given to the dependent relatives of a resident of Newfoundland on active service in our naval or military forces. I understand that there are a number of these men, more particularly in the naval force, and we desire to treat their relatives in the same manner as those of Canadian residents on active service.
Under the present Act the Corporation has no power to give any assistance to members of the Canadian expeditionary forces who have become incapacitated during the war and returned to Canada. Its powers are limited to giving assistance to the wives, children and dependent relatives of men on actual service. Again, under the Act as it now stands, there is no power to give assistance to the wives, children and dependent relatives of men who have been killed on active service. The present amendment will give the Corporation these powers. With regard to the power to assist either men who have been incapacitated and returned to Canada, or widows, children and dependent relatives of men who have been killed, it is provided that this power can be exercised at any time during the war or within six months after the war, but that it shall not be exercisable for a period of more than six months, in favour of any one individual, person or persons, or the relative of any one person or persons; and, further, that it shall not be exercisable in favour of persons who are in receipt of a pension provided by Canada. It is, in effect, intended to cover a period which may elapse after a man has died or become incapacitated and before his dependent relatives, or himself if living, may have established their right to the benefit of a pension that may be provided
either by Canada or by the government of the country in whose service the man may have been. [DOT]
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Guysborough) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 40, to amend the Criminal Code. He said: The object of this Bill is to make it a crime to defraud the Government by the sale of military or navai stores. The word "stores" is used in the Interpretation Act to cover ail articles sold to military or naval authorities.
1 was surprised on examining the criminal code to find that no punishment has been provided for defrauding the Government in this way, although ample provision is made for the punishment of any fraud perpetrated by a man on his fellow man. It is well that parties who attempt to defraud the Government, especially at a time like this, should know that there is a day of reckoning to come. I would give them to understand that, while they may deceive an innocent Minister of Militia or some simple general or colonel in his department, any attempt to defraud the Government may bring them behind the bars of a penitentiary. That is the object of the Bill.
I do not suggest that there are many people practising this kind of fraud in Canada. I do not know, but if some of the public speeches of the Minister of Militia have any weight, there are some at least. I understand the minister proposed that he should be given leave to shoot these swindlers, but I do not propose anything so drastic as that; that looks to me very much like a German move. My proposal is to give them two years behind the bars of some Canadian penitentiary. I am quite well aware that I shall not secure the passage of this Bill without the consent of the Minister of Justice, and I should like to ask him to see that this important and necessary Bill goes through the necessary stages and finally becomes a part of the criminal law of Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
That when this House adjourns this day, it stand adjourned until Thursday next; that Government orders shall have precedence after questions and notices of motions for the production of papers on Thursdays until the end of the session; and that Government orders sha 1 also have the same precedence on Wednesdays as on Thu: sdays until the end of the session; the House to meet at three o'clock on Wednesdays, and the sittings on such Wednesdays to be in all respects under the same rules* provided for other days.
He said: This motion to take Wednesdays and Thursdays for Government business is earlier this session than is usual. I may point out, however, that the session of the Imperial Parliament commenced on the 11th of November and continued to the 27th of that month, when after a session of sixteen days it adjourned until a few days ago. Practically all the time of that session was taken up with Government business, prob-

ably by consent or by some arrangement. Since the session of the Imperial Parliament has been resumed, the entire time has been devoted to Government business. We do not purpose proceeding that far here, as Monday is reserved for private members. There will be also the evenings of Tuesday and Friday for private Bills, and on Wednesdays and Thursdays Government orders are not to be taken up until after notices of motion for production of papers, and questions.

There are really three motions included in this. The first is that the House should not sit to-morrow, Ash Wednesday, and that goes as a matter of course. The other two motions are to take for Government business first the Thursdays, and then the Wednesdays. We on this side of the House have no disposition to interfere with the object which is to be served by this motion, which comes earlier this session than in any other previous session. We know the peculiar circumstances under which we are meeting, and we find no fault with the proposition generally speaking. Under the Rules of the House Thursday becomes a Government day automatically after the House has been in session for a month, and then, in about the sixth week of the session, the Government moves to take Wednesday, whereas that motion is now made in what is practically the second week of the session. Private members will under this motion be deprived of every day except Monday, and consequently there are several important matters on the Order Paper which will not come up this session, amongst others the Bill of Mr. Bradbury, which has been to-day referred to a special committee, the Bill of Mr. Armstrong to amend the Railway Act, the resuming of the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Bickerdike on his Bill relating to capital punishment, an important Bill to amend the Criminal Code, introduced by Mr. McCraney, a Bill by Mr. Maclean (York),, to amend the Railway Act, and the resuming of the adjourned debate on the proposed resolution of Mr. Lemieux with regard to copyright. My suggestion to my right hon. friend is that he should not take next Thursday, when these Bills can probably be discussed.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
A few days ago a fair wage officer residing in Vancouver .advised me that twenty miners had been drowned in one of the Pacific Coast Coal Company's mines at South Wellington, Vancouver Island. He was
instructed to proceed at once to South Wellington and advise us as to conditions there. One of the expert officers of the Department of Mines was also instructed to go to South Wellington. Later I received another message from the fair wage officer saying that the accident had occurred in "this way. There was an old mine, worked out many years ago and was full of water, near the mine that was being opened. The miners working at a lower level in the new mine had broken through into the old mine, and the water in the latter had rushed into the new mine, in which there were ninety-eight men working. Seventy-eight of them escaped, but the remaining twenty were drowned. The officer also advised me that nothing could be done by way of an investigation until the mine was pumped out; that was being done, but that it would require several weeks to empty the mine. It is the intention of the provincial government to make a thorough' investigation, and it is our intention that an expert of the Department of Mines shall attend that investigation in an advisory capacity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend the leader of the Opposition has asked me to make a statement with regard to the changes in the Ministry which have taken place since the session of August last. Two changes have taken place, as my right hon. friend and hon. members generally are aware. Mr. Pelletier, who was Postmaster General from the time that we took office until some time in October last, felt that his physical strength was not equal to the further performance of the very arduous duties imposed upon him as the head of that important department. I know personally that he had been advised by his physician from time to time during the past eighteen months that his health would not bear the very severe strain imposed upon it. Those who were colleagues of Mr. Pelletier, and especially I, as head of the Government, have reason to know that he applied himself to the duties of his office with a vigour and an industry -which perhaps have never been surpassed by a member of any administration since Confederation. I do not think it is too much to say that no minister at the head of the Post Office Department has ever proved himself more capable as an administrator than Mr. Pelletier. The correspondence

which has taken place between Mr. Pelletier and myself has been laid upon the table of the House.
The former Minister of Inland Revenue, Mr. Nantel, has also retired from the Government and has been appointed to a position on the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. The position which he now fills had formerly been occupied by Mr. Bernier, at one time a member of the late Administration, whose health in recent years prevented him from giving to the discharge of his duties the attention which he would undoubtedly have desired to give. Mr. Nantel, as head of the Department of Inland Revenue, occupied himself very closely and assiduously with the duties of his department, and the correspondence which took place between him and myself upon the occasion of his retirement has been placed upon the table of the House.
Mr. Casgrain, who succeeds Mr. Pelletier as Postmaster General, has had a long service in public life, although in recent years it has been interrupted for a considerable period.
Both in the Legislature of Quebec and in the parliament of Canada he had been a distinguished figure years before he made his re-entry into public life as Postmaster General. I have no doubt he will give to the duties of his department the same indefatigable attention, and that he will bring to them the same ability, as characterized the administration of his predecessor.
Mr. Nantel, as Minister of Inland Revenue, has been succeeded by Mr. Blondin, a man whose services in public life have not been nearly so long as that of Mr. Pelletier, as he came into Parliament only in 1908. During the past three yeafs, having been selected to occupy the position of Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees, he has displayed, sometimes under very difficult conditions, an ability, discretion and good judgment which I am sure must haye commended themselves to the members of the House without exception. I have no doubt that in his new position as a responsible minister of the Crown he will display the same qualities and will give to the public service of the country an administration which will commend itself to the judgment of all.

The explanations which have been given to the House by my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) have been copious in words though absolutely lacking in substance. He has told us what everybody who reads the news-
papers already knew that there have been two vacancies and that they have both been filled. I have no exception to take to what he said of Mr. Pelletier, as to his ability and vigour. Mr. Pelletier was well known to us who come from Quebec as a man of ability, and those who did not come from that province were soon convinced of hi* ability when they saw him in office. As to his vigour, especially in the line of dismissals, I do not think, it was exceeded even by any of those who still remain on the Treasury Benches. I have known Mr. Pelletier for a great many years, and I think I can do him no injustice if I add to what has been said about his qualities that he is also possessed of qualities which find expression in the maxim, " What we have we'll hold." He never was known willingly to give up what he had obtained. It was a surprise to us who knew his good points and his weaker points that he had made up his mind to' resign his office. Some there were who remembered that Mr. Pelletier had carried on his campaign in 1911 on the policy of no participation by Canada in the wars of Great Britain, and that the Canadian navy should be destroyed unless the scheme were approved by a plebiscite; who remembered also that, after having taken office he went to his constituents for re-election, he promised that he would obtain a plebiscite or something better. When something better did not come, some there were who proposed that he should do what Mr. Monk had done, and withdraw. Others remembered that when he went for re-election, and afterwards, he more than once told the people of Quebec that as he had agreed to have the shops of the Transcontinental removed from the line of the Transcontinenetal to the line of the Canadian Northern railway, some nine miles from the Transcontinental line, he would see to it that the line of railway, which runs in the valley of the St. Lawrence river, and the shops which are in the valley of the St. Charles river would be connected by a tunnel; but, finding that the Minister of Railways was obdurate and would not agree to the tunnel, finding, as I should say if the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) were present, that the minister had hardened the heart of Quebec, he thought that it was due to his honour not to remain in a Government in which he could not have his wishes and promises carried out. But all these suppositions were wrong. The true reason of the removal, or rather resignation, of Mr. Pelletier is to be found in his ill-health. All were certainly sorry

to hear that Mr. Pelletier's health was not equal to the duties he had undertaken to perform. But their feelings were relieved when they found that, though he was too ill to be a minister of the Crown, at least he could serve the people as a judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec. It is singular how bad health will affect individual cases when, unfortunately, it comes to gentlemen on the other side of the House. Here is Mr. Pelletier unable to serve the country as a minister of the Crown but still with health enough to be a judge of the Superior Court of Quebec; and here is my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) unable to serve the country as a judge and serving the country as a minister of the Crown. This is a. fortunate condition of things which may not be quite plain to the common understanding, but it can be explained by the flexible and elastic logic of the Conservative party, which can always find a solution of every difficulty, and find it on the profitable side.
With regard to the successor of Mr. Pelletier, Mr. Casgrain, I have only a word to say. In my humble judgment he was the logical appointment under the circumstances. Mr. Casgrain has always been a Tory, an undiluted Tory. If he were here, I am sure he would not object to that compliment; or reverse of compliment. He is certainly entitled to the credit-or discredit- of having been under all circumstances a pure, undiluted Tory. He never served the new gods whose stars have risen on the horizon; he was always faithful to his old convictions. I give him full credit for that. He and I are old friends. It is a pleasure personally, though I must say the reverse of a pleasure politically, to see him where he is. And I am sure that the statement of my right hon. friend as to Mr. Casgrain's ability to fulfil the duties of his office will be realized. As to his political views or convictions I cannot say much; they are the misfortune of his circumstances.
There is another change. Mr. Nantel also has been called away from the floor of Parliament and removed to another sphere. It is not my intention to say anything of the removal.of Mr. Nantel from office, but I may have something to say as to the choice of his successor, the present incumbent of the office, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin). It seemed an evidence of the irony of fate that the hon. member for Champlain, the arch-Nationalist, should have been introduced into this House by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), the arch-14
Imperialist. When, on the opening of the session, I saw the new minister walking into this House leaning upon the arm of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce showed by the way he seemed to be limping that he had a heavy load to carry. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has always been an insistent advocate of imperialism. I cannot say as much of his new colleague; but perhaps, after all, there may be within the ranks of the Conservative party, as there is somewhere else, some joy over the conversion of one sinner. The Minister of Inland Revenue was introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. When he told you, Sir, that that hon. gentleman had taken the oath and had signed the roll, I thought he would add that the hon. gentleman had filled up the holes in the flag and that he would now breathe the atmosphere of liberty. But he did not, and really there was no necessity.for his doing so. The hon. member for Champlain is now breathing the atmosphere of office; he has found an atmosphere which is suitable to him, and he can breathe freely, whether there are holes in the flag or not. I have only this to observe: when my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue, then the hon. member for Champlain, was making the speeches which he did make in the province of Quebec; when he was threatening to destroy the Canadian navy when he had an opportunity of doing so, I never believed that he meant one-half of what he said. I always supposed, and rightly supposed, that what he was after was simply to create advantage for himself and for his party. He has succeeded. He is now in office, but to attain office he has travelled a very dangerous road. He has sown the seed of discord -and these appeals to passion are always sure to bring forth a crop of prejudices. My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue is a young member of this House; perhaps he will permit me to say, since he now has the responsibility of office, that he had better always stand by true principle.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If there were wanting evidence of how absolutely at a loss the right hon. gentleman is to find unfavourable comment to make upon the resignation of my hon. friend Mr. Pelletier and his nomination to the Bench, it certainly would be found in the fact that he could not do so otherwise than by making a statement in this House



which is absolutely and unqualifiedly untrue.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen will allow me to say what I wish to say-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I only wish to remind the hon. member that to make the assertion that another member said what was untrue knowing it to be untrue, is not parliamentary.
Take it back.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I said that the statement was untrue; if I had been allowed to proceed I think it would have appeared that I was not stating that the right hon. gentleman knowingly stated what was untrue. If- I may be permitted to complete my phrase, I think I shall be able to put before this House what are the actual facts and at the same time be within the limit of parliamentary rules. I was going on to say that the right hon. gentleman ought to have known the assertion to be untrue. I say that because, Mr. Speaker, every man who knows me, and who knows the circumstances under which I resigned my position on the bench-and I thought until to-day that I might count the right hon. gentleman among them-knows that in connection with my resignation there never was a question, in any manner, shape or form, of illness on my part, or of illness incapacitating me from my. duties on the bench. The letter in which I tendered my resignation is on record in the Department of Justice, and I defy my right hon. friend to find in that resignation the slightest suggestion of illness on my part. I tendered my resignation without the slightest suggestion that I was ill, and I asked for nothing when I tendered that resignation; I simply pointed out that under the express law of this country-a law enacted long before I was born-my fifteen years upon the bench of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec entitled me to the annuity for which that statute provided. I tendered my resignation to take effect when
4 p.m. that right was recognized, and the Government of which the right hon. gentleman was the leader recognized that right by accepting my resignation; yet the right hon. gentleman ventures to-day to make the assertion that he has made. I recall a previous occasion when the right hon. gentleman made the same statement-or, let me correct myself, when it was reported that the right hon. gentleman made the statement. That was in 1908, when I ventured to comply with the

request of what proved to be the larger number of the voters in the division which I have the honour to represent, and to present myself for election to this House. It was then reported in all the papers-among them the papers supporting the right hon. gentleman-that he made in that election campaign a statement similar to the one that he has made here to-day. At that time I took occasion to point out precisely what had occurred; to point out that my resignation, as I said a moment ago, had no connection with any illness or any pretension of illness on my part, and to point out publicly through the press that all the friends of the right hon. gentleman in the province of Quebec, if he did not, knew that perfectly. I can see before me gentlemen with whom I was, as I am glad to say I am to-day, upon terms of friendly intimacy, who sit upon the other side of the House, and who knew me then and knew that I was not ill, and had made no suggestion and no pretension that I was ill. I published that assertion, and the right hon. gentleman has not come back to it until this late date. I may say that afterwards the right hon. gentleman denied having found fault with me in connection with my resignation at that time. What light has come to him since, that he makes the assertion that he has made to-day?
It is certainly a pitiable sight; the leader of a great party compelled to resort to making statements of fact which certainly he cannot know to be true, and which, as I say, the public documents on record in the Department of Justice of this country, the documents forwarded to the Minister of Justice of the Government of Which he was the chief, demonstrate to be false; and that for the petty purpose of making some jeering remarks both with regard to myself, who, thank God, enjoyed at the time I retired from the bench, as I am glad to say I enjoy to-day, the very best of health, and at the expense of my friend the late Postmaster General, with regard to whom I am satisfied that every one who knew him knew that his health during all the time he was- with us left much to be desired. When he left us it was in that position that while his medical adviser would not take the responsibility of counselling him to continue to give constant and arduous and unremitting attention every moment to the numerous details which his duty in the position which he occupied imposed the obligation of looking after, we all know that it is not inconsistent with that, that the hon. gentleman should have been capable of doing the

work that would fall to his lot in the position which he is now filling, work of a totally different kind.
I do not know that there is anything I can add to what I have said. I have heard whisperings of what the right hon. gentleman has said to-day from other people before. I thought the right hon. gentleman was a bigger man than they are, but I find to-day that he has chosen to -put himself upon a level with them. It is a matter, of course, for his own choice to determine. In making the statement which he has made, I am bound to assume that he did not know what he ought to have known; but the thing that outstands is that the statement is absolutely untrue, and that if I am entitled to receive what I am receiving to-day, it is purely and simply that, as recognized by the Government of the right hon. gentleman, as recognized in particular by the	gentleman who in
that Government held the office which I hold, as it must be recognized by any man who can read a statute, that the contract under which I was appointed to the Bench of the Superior Court gave me the same absolute right to receive the pension it provides for on condition that I gave fifteen years of my life to service in that court as it gave me to any dollar of salary which I drew while I sat upon that Bench. I say the truth of that statement does not rest on my word; it rests upon the public record of my resignation, and its acceptance by his Government, and it is justified by the. express provision of the statute law of this country. I do not think there could be any more complete demonstration of the untruth of any statement susceptible of being made than that which I trust I have made of the untruth of the statement of the right hon. gentleman.

In reply to the hon. gentleman's explanation, I just wish to say that I knew, as everybody knows, that the law of the land allows a judge, when he has served fifteen years, if he does not find 'himself equal to the task, to ask for his pension; but I should suppose that if he found himself equal to the task, rather than take the pension he would continue to discharge the duties of his office. The minister has told us that he accepted the pension being in perfect health. I accept his explanation; every one will accept it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I rise for the purpose of saying that the right hon. gentleman, to bolster up his statement, has had to misstate the provision of the statute.

Just a word about the retirement of my good friend the ex-Postmaster General. I quite agree that the Hon. Mr. Pelletier left office because he was in poor health. But if he was in poor health, everybody knows that he is a rich man. I am surprised to find that now, after ihe has retired from the Government and is a judge of the land, receiving $7,000 a year and a pension after fifteen years at his sweet will, that the mail clerks, who earn something like two or three dollars a day, who have large families and get no pension, are called upon to raise a fund for the Hon. Mr. Justice Pelletier. I have received protests from some mail clerks who are indignant at the audacity of some sycophants around the Post Office Department in Ottawa who are trying to raise a fund for the Hon. Mr. Pelletier. I state the simple truth when I say that everybody knows that Mr. Pelletier is a very rich man. Here is a circular- and I call the attention of the right hon. gentleman to this-issued from Ottawa and dated January 14, 1914. It is as follows:
Appreciation for the Honourable Louis P. Pelletier, the friend of the man in the service.
Ottawa, January 14, 1914.
To Postmasters, Chief Clerks, Inspectors, Superintendents, Officers, Clerks and employees of the Post Office Department.
A few months ago some admirers of the Honourable L. P. Pelletier revived the idea of a testimonial to Mr. Pelletier in view of the great sympathy he had always shown towards the best interests of his department during his term as Postmaster General. Released from the cares of office Mr. Pelletier is now free to accept such a testimonial of our esteem, which was impossible while he was a minister of the Crown.
At the convention of the Civil Service Federation held in Ottawa, January 7, 8, and 9, the following committee was entrusted with the completion of the work: F. Grierson, G. Carpenter, J. C. O'Connor, C. A. Halladay, W. J. P. Cantwell, postal clerk, and Wm. Hoop, President Dominion Federation of Letter Carriers, Winnipeg. The committee found the work well advanced but wish to afford an opportunity to all the members of the department to subscribe.
Will you, therefore, constitute yourself the local treasurer of the fund, afford those in your branch or district an opportunity of subscribing, and forward the amount received without delay to the treasurer, C. A. Halladay, Railway Mail Service, at Ottawa, or to any of the above named committee. Small individual contributions only are requested, and all must be in the hands of the treasurer by April 15, 1915, on which day the fund will be closed.
Signed on behalf of the committee.
G. A. Carpenter,
Chairman,
Dead Letter Office, Montreal.
C. A. Halladay, Secretary-Treasurer, Railway Mail Service, Ottawa.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the date?

It is dated 1914, but I think from the context it should be 1915.
I have received protests from some of the unfortunate mail clerks who are being mulcted in this way, and in these hard times, for the benefit of a very wealthy citizen of this country, Hon. Mr. Pelletier. Here is a letter from Kingston in reply to Mr. Halliday, the man who is passing the hat.
I have a circular letter signed by you asking for contributions from the mail clerks for a fund for the benefit of Hon. Mr. Justice Pelletier. I did not know he was in need of this * widow's mite ' from his late employees. If such is not the case and a few of his personal friends or those receiving special favours choose to make a personal presentation, then it is their business; but if it is to be made in the name of the service, then I think you have your nerve with you to undertake to speak for them.
Who signed the letter?

I will show my hon. friend the letter. I do not want this man to be dismissed. The idea of raising such a fund for Hon. Mr. Pelletier from the letter carriers and mail clerks passes my comprehension. It is simply a hold-up and an evidence of sycophancy on the part of those who are getting up the fund, and I am quite sure that if the Hon. Mr. Pelletier knew about it he would stop it at once.
Do not be too sure.

Yes, I must give the
devil his due. We are all being asked to contribute to one thing or another nowadays. There is the Patriotic Fund, the Belgian Relief Fund, subscriptions to hospitals and the Red Cross, and is the poor mail clerk and letter carrier to be asked to stretch the last stitch in his purse and to give his mite to the Hon. Mr. Pelletier, who is worth many hundreds of thousands of dollars? I am quite sure that if he knew about this fund he would give orders for the hold-up to be stopped at once. I hope that the right hon. gentleman will see that this circular does not circulate any more, and that orders are given to the young man whose name appears on this circular to stop soliciting subscriptions at once.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not understand that I have anything to do with it. I never heard of it before. The movement originated, as I gather from the remarks of my hon. friend, in the Civil Service Federation, which is not an official organization at all. Any person who receives a circular

would be absolutely at liberty to disregard it, and his disregard of it would not have the smallest effect in the world upon his status in the Civil Service.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
Department of Trade and Commerce

Deputy Minister, $5,000.	,
["I shall be better able to discuss the matter when the item comes up for consideration.\nAt six o'clock, the House resumed and then took recess.\nThe House resumed at 8 o'clock."]

There are two mistakes on this page which I wish to correct. In the 12th line it reads, '1 at $931 50"; that should be $937 50. In the Census and Statistics Branch, in line 10, it reads, "5 at $1,500"; that should be 5 at $1,050. These are just mistakes in printing.

The number of clerks
appears to have been increased.
The work of the department has been very greatly increased and I had to add three clerks in the lower grade.
Where does the increased work come in?

It comes in from all branches. I should think I would be perfectly safe in saying that in the last six months or a year the work we have been doing in that department, counted by our communications in and out and general activities, has been pretty nearly twice as great as in the preceding year. That is a large statement to make but it is fairly well-borne out by the facts. Especially within the last six months the correspondence has been overwhelming.
Where does it come from?
From all over.

Is it on
account of the expansion of trade or in consequence of the war?

It is because of the larger number of inquiries resulting from conditions brought about by the war. Commercial questions, questions in reference to internal and external trade have multiplied exceedingly. The bulletin which had a very small circulation previously has now a very large circulation. My own particular part of the work is very much more onerous than it has ever been before

21a
in my experience in that department or in any other department with which I have been connected.
Has work previously performed by other departments been transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce?
That was done two years ago.

I quite believe that the work of the department has materially increased, but I think it is a bad year to increase expenses in any department, and that it would be better to keep the work of the department down in some way or make those on the staff work harder.

My officers are working for all they are worth and a great many of them are working overtime; I will tell my hon. friend what I would do if I had a free hand. I would add $100,000 to this department and I would put it this year and next year into the commerce side of the department, and I would do that because I believe that the activities to be developed in connection with the general work of the country, owing to the dislocation of trade, the openings for trade and the vast number of inquiries coming from every part, would justify it. If it were not that financial matters are in such a stringent condition I would ask my colleagues for a 'large increase in this vote and I would use it I think to the great good of the country.

Could not the minister
make some arrangement by which part of the clerical work could be done by some other department where the business has fallen off, for example, the Customs Department, the revenue of which is some $30,000,000 less than formerly, and which . cannot have anything like the necessity for the same clerical staff it had when there was an abounding and expanding revenue, as was the case under the previous Government? I speak of this because in this time of stress, when the Minister of Finance is obliged to impose what he, improperly I think-if I could use the emphatic language of the Minister of Justice, untruthfully I think-calls a war tax, which is striking everybody in this country, striking people who cannot afford to pay it, it does not seem to be a proper time to increase the expenses of administering the different departments. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is adding to the items on page
27 of the Estimates altogether pretty close to $12,000, which is a pretty heavy jump for one year, particularly a year like the present, when everybody in this country feels the necessity of curtailing. People who could very well make use of more employees in their business are cutting down the number of hands employed by them; they are doing more work themselves, they are spending longer hours at their business, in order to economize, and yet we find the Government instead of economizing going on increasing the expenditure of this department. Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce noticed the Ottawa Citizen of this morning, which refers to the addition of a number of employees and consequent very great increase in expenditures? The Citizen quotes from a statement made by Prof. Shortt, the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, at a meeting a short time ago, as to which the Citizen says:
Prof. Shortt referred to the return brought down in Parliament a few days ago, showing the names of 2.000 men who had been dismissed since the change of government. Who, asked the Speaker, took the places of the 2,000? The answer was 10,000.
It is a great pity that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has been usually recognized as being pretty economical-perhaps the economical member of the Government-has not had some supervision over these other departments in which such an enormous increase in the number of employees has taken place. If that statement of Prof. Shortt is true, what does it mean? It means that, since this Government has come into power, during a considerable part of which time business has been depressed and times have been hard, if the statement of Prof. Shortt is true, there has been added to the employees of the Government the enormous number of 8,000. Assuming that their average salary would be $1,000-1 do not imagine that would be too large a figure-it would mean an addition of $8,000,000 to the expenditure of the country. Prof. Shortt, the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, is regarded as being very careful and accurate in what he says; and, if his statement is correct, this is rather an alarming state of affairs. Surely that expenditure might be avoided. Surely it is better to put up-, with some inconvenience; surely it is. better for the clerks already in the service; to work a little harder and for the ministers and deputy ministers to give a little more attention to their departments, than to go on so rapidly increasing expenditure.

It is hardly fair to.
Charge the Minister of Trade and Commerce with this large addition to the service, because he is not by any means the greatest offender. I find, on examining the return, that in the Department of Trade and Commerce there were thirteen dismissals and forty-nine appointments during the present Administration. Some of the other departments, however, have gone much further than that in the number of appointments. The Department of Customs has dismissed 271 persons and appointed 1,649. The Department of Indian Affairs has dismissed 135 and appointed 295. The Department of Inland Revenue has dismissed 73 and appointed 291. The Department of the Interior has dismissed 309 and appointed 1,651. The Department of Justice has dismissed 20 and appointed 257.
With immigration falling off.

The Department of
Public Works is perhaps the greatest offender of all, with 511 dismissals and 2,002 appointments.
Shocking!

The Department of the Secretary of State has dismissed 20 and appointed 287. The Department of Railways has dismissed 363 and appointed 2,076. The total number of dismissals is 2,115 and the total number of appointments 10,576.

What about the Post
Office Department?
I have not the figures.

They did not dismiss
any.

In observing the remarks of Prof. Shortt in regard to the subject to which the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has drawn attention,
I noticed that the return said nothing whatever of retirements; and I myself was rather surprised that a man in the position which Prof. iShortt occupies should, with a return in that form, give the impression which would evidently be gathered from his words as reported in the press. During the discussion which may ensue on the words of the hon. member for St. John, it should be kept in mind ithat, whatever explanation there may be, tthe fact appears very patently that no account is taken of the very great number which there must be of retirements.

How many would there
be?
Would the hon. member expect me to answer that?	[DOT]
Fifty at the most.
I think those who affect to speak publicly on the subject should know before they speak.

When my hon. friend
the Solicitor General says there are a great many retirements, he ought to be able to give us an idea of the number, if it be around 25 or 50 or 100.

Will the minister indicate to the committee what his staff is doing in the matter of seeking new outlets for Canadian trade? He has informed us that his department is extremely busy at one thing or another in consequence of the unsettled trade conditions, but he has not given us any definite idea as to the nature of the work his department is doing.

Perhaps my hon. friend would rather take the items as they come under the regular heads. There is a vote which will come up shortly for trade commissioners, to which appertains chiefly the extension of trade. It would be better if the discussion would come up on that.

I think this is the proper place, because we are asked to vote these increases in salaries upon the ground that extra work has been thrown upon the department by reason of trade conditions. The Minister of Trade and Commerce usually gets through his estimates very quickly, and we may never again have an opportunity to have this explanation. It need not be a lengthy one.

I was a little
amused at my hon. friend the member for St. John, who professed to be greatly alarmed at the increase of expenditures shown in this modest estimate of mine.
This is only a sample.

Verily some
great change must have taken place in my hon. friend during the last five or six years if he has learned now to be afraid of a small increase occasioned by the appointment of four or five clerks, mostly of low grade. My memory is fairly good; and I think I have been in the House when my hon. friend has come down, not only in connection with

his own estimates, but in company with his colleagues, and has asked for far larger increases, and he has never shown the least sign of alarm in his countenance.

Those were prosperous
times.	_

But my hon.
friend is taking fright at so small a bogey as is before him at the present moment. I would like to know what will become of him when he approaches some of my colleagues, of whom he has been speaking to-day, and comes up against what my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has stated to be very large increases. It is not very fair that the brunt of this should come against the least offending one, according to my hon. friend's own contention. I have, however, always been used to taking a heavy burden on my shoulders.
Sin no more. ,

I have appointed to permanent positions three clerks, who have been in the service of the department for a number of years at $500 each. Then there is an appointment, in the Census and Statistics branch, one in the third division; but while there is an appointment of one extra in that division, a very large number have been dropped out from the non-permanent statistical work on account of the work which had been apportioned to them in the way of tabulations and such like having been performed. But there is always a certain amount of work which remains over for file clerks after these tabulations have been made.
The one appointment that was made here is to keep up with that extra work. If my hon. friend insists that I should go into a disquisition to-day on general trade matters, of course I shall have to oblige him but he would oblige me if he would leave it over until the time when the principal items of the Trade and Commerce Estimates come up. I shall show to better advantage at that time.
Canada's proportion of expenditure in connection with International Customs Tariffs Bureau, $662.
This is the International Customs Bureau which has been in operation for eight or ten years.
Is that the one with its head office in Brussels?

Yes. Since the war commenced it has not been carrying on its work, but we hope there will be an end to the war, and when that comes this work will be taken up -again, I suppose.
Gold and Silver Marking Act, $4,000.

This work is carried on by our inspector, Mr. W. J. Ryan, of Toronto. He has been in charge of the work since the Act came into force. His salary is $2,000 a year. He was formerly an official of the Department of Agriculture for this same work, which has been transferred to my department.
West India cable, $38,932.33.
Has there been any addition to the length of cable provided lor this service?

No.
Supervision of lake and ocean freight rates,

This is a vote I took last year for the purpose of employing an officer with expert knowledge, and at the same time practical knowledge, of freight rates, particularly of ocean rates and also rates by lake and river, in connection chiefly with the trade from the Great Lakes to and across the Atlantic. I explained last year why I wanted the vote and it was given me by the House, but it has been impossible for me to find a really good man whose services I could get, and so I have not made the appointment. I do not intend to fill the position until I find the one whom I consider to be the proper man; and it is

sometimes difficult to engage such a man, because they are not usually idle but are taken up by the great transportation companies, and it is difficult to get them at a fair salary. However, communications are now in progress which I think will result in my being able to find a man for the position.
Does this vote coyer salary alone ?

Salary and
general expenses.
How is it intended to supervise ocean freight ?

As the hon. gentleman is aware, the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes a great many of these steamship contracts and provides the lines with subsidies, and has to oversee the service itself. I was successful in getting a very good man to take in charge the supervision of the service in Canada on both coasts and also the inland services that were subsidized. But in these contracts ' there is a clause which gives the Minister of Trade and Commerce the power to fix rates. So I find myself obliged to make decisions of that kind yet without the technical and expert advice necessary to give what I think a reasonable judgment. What I wished was expert advice upon which I could rely in enforcing these clauses of the contracts. A layman who has to deal with these matters finds it difficult to follow the intricacies of transport rates by 'land or sea. It is one of the most difficult and 'complex subjects that I ever attempted to get some knowledge of. The object then, of the vote is to get an advisor or expert who can inform the department and the minister with reference to these matters.
Why not call in an expert each time you require one?

If my hon.
friend had charge of the department I do not think he would be able to do that very well. Invariably the expert would be connected with a transportation company; one would need to enlist the services of an expert receiving salary or emolument not from these companies, but from the department.

Would it not be possible for my hon. friend to avail himself of the services of Mr. Hardwell or some of the other experts of the Board of Railway Com-

missioners to deal with these particular matters?

I think their
time is pretty well taken up. I talked that over with the Chairman of the Railway Board; there are many things in respect of which we could co-operate if we had an expert of that kind in connection with ocean services.

The minister stated that under the mail contract there is power on the part of the department to regulate and control freight rates. I should like to ask my hon. friend if he has taken any steps to regulate ocean freights in respect of subsidized mail steamers during the past six months. It appears that the rate on lumber shipped to the United Kingdom, which a year or two ago was 36 shillings per standard of lumber, to-day is 100 shillings. That, of course, very seriously interferes with the export of lumber to the United Kingdom. The freight charges made by the subsidized steamers naturally have a very considerable effect upon the charges made by steamers which do not belong to the regular lines and which are not subsidized.

I think my hon. friend will recognize that the last six months have been a very difficult and stormy period in which to try to regulate ocean freight rates; the causes for this condition my hon. friend very well knows. Our subsidized steamship lines crossing the Atlantic were levied on by the British Government, owing to the necessity for securing transports, and were time after time much reduced in their bests vessels. All the great lines had their best vessels taken aw,ay from them, and they had to get such vessels as they could find. This disorganized and confused the service. These somewhat extraordinary causes and others, operating together, brought about a great scarcity of ocean tonnage, and freight rates have gone up in all parts of the world. It has been absolutely impossible for the Government to get, even for its own purposes, for the transport of war supplies, vessels at anything like the proper time or at anything like reasonable rates. If I had had all the experts available,
I do not think I would have endeavoured very much during the past five months to regulate ocean freights. As to our main subsidized companies, we have been keeping in constant touch with them and, so far as possible, consulting with them in the matter of rates. So far as our subsidized ser-

vices from Montreal, Halifax and St. John are concerned, whilst the rates have increased, I do not think they will increase abnormally. Certainly they have not done so, compared with increases that have taken place in all parts of the world.

I think that freights on lumber have been subjected to an increase of about 150 per cent.
Mr. 'SINCLAIR: There is another reason for the increase in freight rates upon lumber with which my hon. friend, perhaps, is not familiar. Under the system that prevails in the province of New Brunswick and in some of the Maritime provinces, lumber cargoes taken across to England invariably fall short in measurement. The man who undertakes to carry a cargo of lumber to Great Britain expects to incur a loss; that - is, when he reaches the other side he expects to find that he is a number of standards short of the quantity he was supposed to carry, and the lumber people on the other side compel him to bear that loss, which usually amounts to a very considerable sum. The consequence is that the difficulties which are encountered come back on the lumber people. No ship-owner wants to carry lumber 'across the water, because he knows that he will have to meet the loss occasioned by shortage when he lands on the other side. An attempt was made to rectify this a few years ago. I had the honour of introducing a measure amending the law so as to make the shipowner responsible only for the number of pieces delivered to him at the point of shipment, thus relieving him from any liability for loss after having reached the other side. It is impossible to
5 p.m. measure lumber when it is placed on board ship. It comes down the St. John or some other river in scows or schooners; the ship is always in a hurry to leave, and to put the scale on each board or plank would be an endless and practically impossible task. The consequence is that the shipowner has to take the measurements given him by the merchant and is victimized when he reaches the other side with his cargo. When the measure to which I have referred was introduced in the House, the lumbermen, especially of new, Brunswick, came here in great numbers and insisted upon the restoration of the old law, which obliged the ship-owner to sign for the number of feet stated by the owners to have been delivered to him. Consequently the law is the same as it was before; ships are scarce and rates high, and the lumber owners are themselves to blame for their present difficulties.
I would point out to the minister, too, that if he employs an expert, that expert should not only be engaged in ascertaining the proper rates, but should be able to report to the minister as to whether or not subsidies should be granted in particular instances. Many of the subsidies have been on the list for twenty or twenty-five years, and some of them should not be granted.
I have no hesitation in saying that subsidies are granted by this House that should not be granted and would not be granted by the minister if he knew all the facts.
I realize the importance of obtaining information as to freight rates, but the matter to which I now refer is also an important phase of the work of the department.
Department of Customs-salaries, 5323,375 ; contingencies, $20,000.
Why, witn a declining revenue, is it necessary to increase the staff?
We are not increasing the staff. Last year we had a staff of 245 and this year we have the same number.
There is an increase of nearly $8,000.
That is the statutory increase only. We have the same number of employees, but one clerk in the third division, subdivision A, is replaced by one in the third division subdivision B.

I suppose that it seems
rather harsh to dispense with some of these people, but the customs have fallen off enormously. Could not the minister shift some of his staff over to say the Militia Department? There must be many in his department who are practically idle.

Of course, quite a number
have gone to the war. Seventy-six employees of the Customs, inside and outside, have enlisted.

What ' is the rule
adopted with regard to employees of the Government who have volunteered for foreign service? Do they get their full salary?
So far as the customs officials are concerned, any who have asked to be allowed to go to the war and who have obtained permission from the department are paid their salaries in full.

The reason I ask is that I have heard lately that quite a number of the employees of the Intercolonial Railway volunteered for service, and they make

the statement in the press that they were assured by the Intercolonial authorities that they would receive their full pay while on serivce. The have latterly been informed that the Minister of Railways has refused to carry out the arrangement that was made with them by the general manager. They feel very much aggrieved at the treatment they are receiving, which they claim is harsh and, apparently from the statement of the Minister of Customs, is entirely different from the treatment meted out to the employees of the branch of the service over which he presides. I think the same rule should apply to all the employees of the Government service. If an employee of the Department of Customs is allowed full pay while on foreign service, I do not see why an employee of another department, such as the Intercolonial, should not be treated in exactly the same way, more especially as they volunteered -under an assurance given to them by the general manager that they would receive full pay.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Was any assurance
given the first contingent?

Personally I do not
know the details, but I saw a statement in the press that the Government had gone back on the promise made by the general manager.

As I understand, in all the departments of the Government, which would include the Intercolonial, all who asked and obtained permission to go to the front would receive their pay in full, and the same applies to the Intercolonial. It was necessary to ask them to apply for permission for the reason that in some cases it was very difficult to allow men to go. There must be some misunderstanding, and I am sure that the Minister of Railways will be able to explain the matter satisfactorily to my hon. friend when the railway estimates come up.

What is the cause of the enormous increase in the number of clerks engaged in the customs during the past three years? The following questions and answers are supplied in a return brought down on the 10th of March, 1914:
Q. How many employees of the Federal Government of Canada, including all services and all departments, have been dismissed from October 10, 1911, to the present date?-A. 271 dismissals.
Q. How many customs employees have resigned?-A. 194 resignations.
Q. How many have deserted the service?- A. 11.

Q. How many deserters have been punished? *-A. None.
Q. How many new employees have been engaged or appointed by the present Government during that period?-A. 1,649.
And it is signed by John McDougald, the Commissioner of Customs. To take on 1,649 new employees there must have been an enormous increase in the work to be done. The most likely explanation is that the Government or the Customs Department have created vacancies in order to find places for 1,649 men who are looking for Government jobs. According to that return, the Minister of Customs has a remarkable knack of making jobs for friends. But the knack is not peculiar to him. The Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works, as a matter of fact, even outstripped him in this respect, but by the pleased look on the minister's face I see he has made up his mind to catch up to them. Seriously, it is an extraordinary state of affairs and requires some explanation. The work must have increased enormously to justify engaging all these new employees.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Does that return include deaths and superannuations? There must have been quite a number of them in that time?
It is up to the department to furnish that information.

The hon. member for
Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) has partly explained the increase. Information was not asked for in the return as to the number of deaths. I can get the numbers, however. During the last two or three years there has been a great deal more to do in the customs on account of the increased revenue, but we never appoint a man at any place unless he is recommended by one of the inspectors. We increased the staff in the town of my hon. friend. Does he complain of that?
That is a very busy point.

And so are other places. New offices have had to be opened and stalls increased all over the Dominion. We are continually being urged to open new offices along the frontier and throughout the West. With the growth of settlement it is absolutely necessary to have more men, but no more are appointed than are actually required; in fact, there are places now along the frontier where men are urgently required.

How many did
you appoint at the request of members?

None, unless there were
vacancies or some new port was opened.

The minister has just stated that he made no appointments except on the report of the inspector. Two years ago I called to his attention the dismissal of a man in my constituency, and was told by the minister that he had been dismissed because there was nothing for him to do. The salary he enjoyed was $100. Another man was appointed for the same job of doing nothing at $250.
Not at the same place?

At the same place. The minister at that time stated that he made the appointment upon the recommendation of the inspector, and I asked him to bring down the inspector's recommendation. The minister was unable to find any recommendation on his file, and said that the man must have been appointed on the verbal report of the Commissioner of Customs. The Commissioner of Customs could not possibly have had any intimate knowledge of the circumstances existing in that remote community, but nothing that I could do could elicit any further information from the minister. As a matter of fact the dismissal was made upon the recommendation of the Conservative candidate, and the new appointment was made on the same recommendation, but with this difference: whereas the former occupant of the office got $100 for doing nothing, the present one does nothing and gets $250 for it. The minister cannot get away from that. There must be thousands of such cases in Canada to account for the extraordinary increase , in salaries of Customs Department employees, and for the extraordinary number that have been appointed to take the place of those who have been dismissed.
Is it customary to punish deserters from the Customs service?
We never have deserters.
If they did desert, would you punish them?
We shall wait for a case.

The minister has stated that a large number of additional employees have been put on by reason of the increased revenue. My hon. friend knows that the revenue has fallen off lately at least 25 per cent. Has there been any corresponding reduction in the number of employees? There must be less work for them to do.
Those 1,600 positions are not all new appointments; deaths and resignations account for some of them.
How many?

I will get that information. Although the revenue has fallen off, at some places it has increased very much and we have had to take on new employees. Then the war came. I do not feel like dismissing these men immediately. I hope the war will not last so very long, and I hardly think it is fair to turn out men with families, -who have been for some time in their positions. While perhaps they have not as much to do as before the war, I believe we should keep them on until at least we see what the conditions will be later. I believe that when the war is over these men will all have as much to do as they had formerly. I have not dismissed any officials on account of the war, but in cases where the revenue of a port has decreased and where there have been resignations at other ports and vacancies caused by men going to the war, I have sent the men from the ports where business has decreased to take their places. I am continuing that practice.
I understand the minister to say that he has paid the salaries to his officials who have gone on active sei'vice.

Instructions were given to
pay every such official his salary and if my hon. friend knows of a case in which that has not been done I should be glad if he would let me know.

I have no information as to that with regard to the Customs Department. I would like to know why what applies to the Customs Department in that respect does not apply to other departments of the Government. I may state that the employees of the Intercolonial railway who have gone on active service have not been paid their salaries. Why are the men belonging to the Department of Customs who have gone to the front paid, while the employees of the Railway Department are not paid?
I am not in a position to answer for the Railway Department. The salaries of all Custom officers who have gone on active service have been paid from the time they left the service up to the present.

Then, it is correct to say that in the Department of Customs ever

since the war broke out there has been no effort made to economize or reduce expenses?

We have tried to economize in every way we could, but in some cases the war as a matter of fact made more work for the officials. We have had to take extra precautions along the frontier. I have done everything to economize other than to dismiss permanent officials. I do not think the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) would urge that I should dismiss wholesale the officials who have been employed for some time. I do not think the hon. gentleman would suggest that under present conditions I should dismiss officials at every port in the country.

I would think that before the Finance -Minister of this Government came to Parliament to impose a very unusual and very heavy tax burden upon the people of this country, there should have been an honest effort made on the part of the different members of the Government to reduce expenses in all the departments, not only in the matter of public works but in the matter of salaries. Apparently, so far as we know at present, there has been no effort to do that, although the Government has resorted to every expedient to impose additional taxes on the people. With a declining revenue it seems to me there ought not to be and would not be nearly as much work to do in the Department of Customs as there was when there was an abounding revenue and when of course there would be need for more help.

Does the minister intend to make any reduction in the cost of administering his department, outside of the salaries of the officials ? The estimates of the department provide for $4,215,000, or an increase of $400,000 over last year, although the revenue this year will be very much reduced.

The hon. gentleman is incorrect in saying that these estimates exceed the estimates of late year by $400,000. The estimates of last year were for $4,210,000, and this year the estimates amount to $4,215,000.
There is an increase anyway. I am sure there could be some means found to reduce the expenditure of the Customs Department by $100,000 or even $200,000.

The increase of $5,000 in these estimates is an amount to be paid to the Department of Justice to be disbursed by it, and on account of secret preventive service. Owing to the war the secret service has been increased, and we are asking for $5,000 more. Outside of that amount we are simply asking -for the same estimates as last year. Of course it does not necessarily follow that we will expend the whole amount of these estimates. If the war keeps on and there are resignations or deaths, we will not replace with new men. I do not think it would be proper for me to decrease these estimates.
Why not ?
I may require them. .

Will the minister tell me later on how many employees there were at the ports of Montreal, Winnipeg, Halifax, Quebec and Toronto when he took office, and how many there were on the 1st of January this year ?
- Mr. REID: I will get the information later.

I would point out to my hon. friends on this side of the House that bad as is this return which they are discussing, it is only a partial return. So far as the Customs Department is concerned, the return is about a year old, being dated March, 1914. The Minister of Customs should give us a supplementary return -showing the state of affairs approximately to date before he proceeds with his estimates.
What is the increase in the number of employees in the Inside Service ?
No increase. We had 245 employees last year, and we are asking for the same number this year.
How many were there before my hon. friend took office ?
In the estimates for 1911-12, 198 were asked for. There has been an increase of 47 since then.
What was the revenue when my hon. friend took office and what is the revenue to-day ?
I have not the figures. The revenue last year was about $30,000,000 more than it was in 1911-12.

Upon what principle does the minister make promotions in posi-

tion and increases in salary in the outside service P I understand, of course, that the Civil Service Act furnishes machinery by which the minister makes promotions in the inside service. Does he receive a report from any official in his department, or is there any well-defined rule by which those promotions are made ?

As has been the practice for many years, the officials of the department prepare a statement for the minister showing the increases they would recommend in the outside service from one end of the Dominion to the other. It has been not only my custom, but that of my predecessor, to follow that practice very closely.

An official of the department making a list of that kind would have some regard for the number of years of service of each officer, for the position which he occupied, and for the salary which he was then receiving. I would imagine that the official who would report to the minister would be an officer of the inside service who would be largely governed by the records of the department. There appears to be some peculiar method by which that official deals with officers in the otutside service. In the town from which I come we have many officers of the Department of Customs.
What town is that ?

The town of North
Sydney, a well-known town in the Maritime provinces. I am sorry that my hon. friend's geography has been so neglected. I find that by some beautiful instinct this inside official passes over the Grits and promotes the Tories in that town. I am rather suspicious that there must be some other influence than that of the inside official. I rather think that the inside official puts himself in touch with the Tory heelers in the town of North Sydney and finds out who are Grits and who are Tories, and that he promotes the Tory over the head of the poor Grit. Such has been glaringly the ease in the town of North Sydney lor the last few years. New men have been appointed at salaries four or five hundred dollars more than the old officials are receiving. That is unworthy of this country and unworthy of the department. The minister should inquire more closely into the knowledge which his inside officer has of these things and into the unfairness of this method of dealing with the officers of this Department.

As regards increases, I find that the statement which the official submits to me is very fair so far as both Liberal and Conservative officers are concerned. We have shown no favour, and I can hardly believe there is an hon. member on the other side who can say that we have not been treating all the officers, irrespective of politics, fairly as far as increases are concerned. I know that increases 'have been given to Liberals as well as to Conservatives in all the ports, including Sydney. The hon. member knows that. If he does not, I have a list of the olncials at Sydney and can show that they have received increases. Of course, there are officers whose salaries are at the maximum for the positions which they hold, and therefore we cannot give them further increases. I have, however, tried to give fair salaries where the salaries were small.
What happens in most of these Customs positions is, I suppose, whiat happened when my hon. friends opposite were in power; that is, if a vacancy occurs, and a person competent to fill it is appointed, that position is generally the one that he gets. That has been the policy of the Liberal party, and I do not see why it should not be the policy of this patty. I am willing to make promotions as far as possible, but if a vacancy occurs in the Customs Department, that is the vacancy the appointee is after, and that is the vacancy he should get if he is qualified to fill the position.

I do not wish to mention any names of officers. If the minister . will familiarize himself with the different names, he will find that some of the old officers are working at small salaries, and that others who have been appointed since the change of Government are getting large salaries and have been receiving their increases from year to year, while the older officers, appointed under the former Administration, are not receiving increases at all.

I will make inquiries. I have a list before me of the officers at North Sydney. There are four or five men there, and they all got increases last year. If these are not all the names, I shall be able to give them to the hon. member later. We gave increases to T. L. Brennan, David Edwards, E. F. Jackson and Angus Young.
Those are the Tory officials.
Are there any Liberal officials there?
Yes; but you will not find their names on the list of those who have received increases.

I would like to ask the Minister in reference to a vacancy in the Customs office at Arichat. The preventive officer there, Captain Lawrence Gerrior, died nearly a year ago, The office has not been filled, and I would like to know if it is the intention of the minister to fill it.

'Not at the present time. I seem to be in a rather awkward position, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) insisting that I shall reduce the staff and the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) insisting that I shall make appointments.
I am not insisting at all, but I would like to know how long the minister will persist in his determination not to fill the office.
I will not fill it until the work requires an officer at that port. .

And that will probably synchronize with the decision of the Tory patronage committee there as to an appointee. They suffer there from an embarrassment of riches-there are about twenty, I understand, applying for the office, backed by their several groups of the patronage committee. Is it because there is no work to do that the position is not filled?
I have decided not to fill it at the present time. We can get along at present without the services of an officer there.
And unless there is evidence that the services of an officer there are necessary, the minister will not fill the position?
No.
You know, we have had instances of men dismissed because there was nothing to do and others appointed at higher salaries to do that nothing.
The minister said some of the, expert officers of his department had gone to the Finance Department?

One man, Mr. Breadner. Mr. Breadner was brought here from Toronto and took a position in the Customs Department. But the Minister of Finance wanted his services in connection with that depart-

ment, and so Mr. Breadner was taken over by the Finance Department, and has ceased to be an officer of the Customs.
Is he the only one?
So far as I know.
His salary is not provided for in these estimates?
No.
Are the officers on the revenue cutters on the coast under the jurisdiction of the Customs Department?

The naval cutter Margaret
was taken over by the Naval Service Department at the outbreak of the war and the ' Customs Department has nothing to do with her at the present time.
I refer particularly to the Alert, a vessel in the service on the coast of Cape Breton.
That is a small vessel, and she is still with the Customs.

I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, for his investigation, certain occurrences on the coast of Cape Breton last year during the time the Alert was in that vicinity. In September, I think it was, a large amount of contraband or smuggled goods was landed at Lingan from a vessel called the Mary. For several days before that, the revenue cutter Alert was in Lingan bay or harbour. The arrival of the Mary containing the smuggled goods synchronized with the departure of the Alert. Now, I am not making any charge, but simply stating a fact when I say that the supposition in that part of the country is that the Alert was called off duty in Lingan bay after having knowledge of the fact that the Mary had left St. Pierre with a load of smuggled liquor. The public in the vicinity of Lingan and New Waterford believe that she was called off by certain political heelers in Cape Breton for the purpose of enabling their friends to land these smuggled goods. Many of the smugglers, it is true, have been convicted and have paid heavy fines. I say I am making no charge, and I am sure no charge has been made against Mr. Angus Young, who is not an officer of the Alert, but an officer of the Customs at North Sydney who was looking after the case in Sydney when these parties were tried. I would like the minister and his department to investigate and investi-

gate thoroughly, the rumours that have been going around in that vicinity as to the negligence and incapacity of the captain, and particularly the evidence of his negligence and incapacity in allowing these contraband goods to he landed at Lingan.

This is the first intimation
I have had of this matter. I have just made inquiry of the commissioner, and he tells me that the parties were prosecuted, and that this vessel, the Mary, which is not worth very much, is under seizure. Until the officers reach a final decision in a case of seizure, the matter does not usually come before the minister. I shall certainly have the matter brought before the commissioner for investigation, and if anything has happened such as the hon. gentleman says, of course we cannot allow that. I think there must be some misunderstanding. The commissioner and the officials of the department have dealt with the matter. However, before we get through with my estimates, and at some future sitting of the committee, I will be in a position to discus's' the matter much better than I can now:
Did the minister say he would investigate it?
Yes.

There were rather extraordinary things in connection with the landing of liquors at Lingan. To begin with, let me tell the minister, that the chief leader of the Tory party at that place has been found guilty of being the leader of this gang of smugglers. It so happens that this landing was made on a beautiful Sunday morning. And the extraordinary thing is that it happened that these goods were landed right at the door of the customs officer at that place. But early on Sunday morning, before seven o'clock, this customs officer was called away, forsooth, by the leading Tory heeler of that town, for a meeting at Glace Bay.
Can the hon. gentleman tell me the name of the officer?	[DOT]

His name is John
Burke. I am not saying he went away, but that he was called away by the chief Tory boss in that vicinity. The absence of the officer and of the Alert seems to synchronize strangely with the landing of the goods.	I am surprised
that the hon. minister has heard nothing of this matter. It took place on Sunday morning, at a time when the Alert had glided away and the customs officer had been carefully stowed away in Glace Bay. The chief performer of the Tory party has since been found guilty of being at the head of the gang.

I shall be better able to discuss the matter when the item comes up for consideration.
