We placed in the Estimates the same amount as for 1914-15, as we had the same number of employees.
What proportion of that is for salaries and what for contingent expenses?
I have a list here of the amounts spent at every port in Canada.
Will the vote be ex hausted at the end of this year?
Yes.
Approximately how much will be spent on contingencies?
I have not separate figures showing that.
The boat service would not come within that item?
No. There is an item below for boats and cruisers.
Can you give us some idea of what' will come under this item besides salaries?
Rent, overtime of officers, expenses in connection with stationery, and so on.

Is there no way in which the minister could reduce this item by a million dollars or so? This item of $3,590,000 for salaries and contingent expenses is more than the total cost of Customs administration in 1913, in which year the total cost was $3,150,000.

The increase in salaries
brings the cost of administration up each year.	'

But the total cost in
1912-	13 was 3,150,000; for 1915-16 you are asking for an amount greater than that, which seems pretty hard to understand.

The revenue was probably $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 more in 1914-15 than in 1911-12. Although the amount expended for the collection of the revenue was more, the percentage of the cost of collection was less. I have a statement showing the percentages for a number of years. In 1912-13 the cost was $274,000, and it was higher in
1913-	14.
Your revenue in 1912-13 was $135,000,000. It was less than that last year.

The revenue in 1912-13 was $115,630,000, and in 1911-12 $87,596,426.40. The increase in the number of officers and in salaries of course makes our expenditures greater. Now that the war is on there is a groat deal more work to do, although the revenue is less. For instance, we could not possibly reduce the staff at Halifax or

Quebec, or Montreal, or Toronto, where many of the extra officers are employed. I do not think any member of this House would ask us to dismiss these men in the winter, especially as their services will probably be required when navigation opens.
You should never have laken them on.

I never took a man on unless he was recommended by the inspector or by the Commissioner or one of the officials of the Department. I was asked a question about Montreal. I never took on a man there unless he was recommended by the collector, Mr. White, or the surveyor, Mr. McLaughlin. I have always tried to keep the staff down.
Two good officers.

There has been quite a growth in Halifax.

That is true, but I do hot
think the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) would say we have too many officials there.

I do not know
about that; I think I could say that. Will the minister tell us how much more it would cost to collect a revenue of one and a half million dollars than it would to collect a revenue of one and a quarter million dollars?
I have not got it down as fine as that. The total collections throughout the Dominion were taken and the ratio was 2.74 which was one of the lowest in the history of the department.
Will the minister implement that statement as soon as possible with the Winnipeg figures?
I shall. The Winnipeg figures were overlooked. I will hand them to the hon. gentleman to-mOrrow.

I understood the minister to say that within the last two years the salaries of Customs officials all over the Dominion have been increased. Has there been any increase of salary granted to Custom officials in the port of Yarmouth within the last few years?
I cannot answer that question now; I have not got it on the list.
I always thought Yarmouth was something of a place, but if the minister has not got it on his list he cannot think much about it.
It is a good port all right.
Have there been any recommendations from Cape Breton county for the appointment of customs officers at New Waterford?
There was a petition some time ago but no action was taken.
Has the minister appointed any new customs officers in North Cape Breton, and if so, where ?
I do not remember of any at the present time. If the hon. gentleman will give, me some more information on the point I may be able to answer him.

The question is fairly explicit. Since last winter has the minister opened any new customs offices in the county of Victoria or North Cape Breton, and if so where ? For example, has he opened a new customs office in Iona in Victoria county; what has been the revenue from this office feince it was opened, and how far is it from the nearest previously existing customs office ?
There has been an office opened at Iona, but what tWe revenue has been I cannot say; I shall send a state-irient of it to the hon. member.

Is it not a fact that this new office is within a mile of another office. It is a very nice country settlement, of course, but usually a country settlement like that is served by one customs house. I understand that about half a mile away from this new customs house 15
is another. What was the urgent necessity for putting a new customs house there when there was one close by ?
Is it not a fact that the old customs house is on the other side of the lake ? I am told there is quite a revenue at that office and it was opened for the convenience of the people.

That remark of the minister would apply to two customs houses at every bridge in the country because one would be at one side of the river and the other would be at the other. This is a -mere narrow arm of the sea where there is a very excellent bridge travelled all the time, and the old office was at one end of the bridge and I understand political necessity made it necessary to open another office at the other end of the bridge. '

It may possibly be true that the old customs house was within half a mile or a mile of the new one, but it is of great convenience to the steamers plying in that locality. Sometimes we have to put these offices close together for the convenience of steamers which run on lakes or rivers so that we may have a preventive officer to clear them in and out, or they could not call at a particular place. As I understood it, if we did not have an officer at this point it would be very inconvenient. At all events, representations were made to. that effect and we opened an office for the convenience of the public and I suppose it is benefiting them.

This bridge to which
the minister refers is a drawbridge and the draw is at the end of the bridge where the old customs office is. For any vessel that wants to enter there, the Government wharf is at the draw end of the bridge. There the vessels had every convenience necessary to depart or enter, as they might deem advisable. On the end where the minister has put his new custom house, there is no draw at all and no vessels go there in the winter time. No vessels will ever go there, so that the building is absolutely away from the market. I do not grudge the people of Iona the convenience of a customs house if it is to be of any use; but I claim that it was put in that- position for a political necessity, to meet a political emergency. Let the minister not try to defend it on any commercial principle whatever.

I understand from the minister's remarks that throughout the



country- there have been general increases in the salaries of the customs officials. On what basis have these increases been made? Have they been made on the basis of length of service? For instance, in any particular customs office there are the collector, the assistant collector and a number of clerks and appraisers. Do the collector and the assistant collector get stated increases by way of an added percentage each year, and does the same rule apply to the clerks and appraisers and under clerks in each office?
Mr. RE'ID: I explained this matter just before recess. The hon. member will understand that in the inside service the statute provides for certain increases'which go into effect at the end of each year. So far as the outside service is concerned, it has been the general rule for the Minister of Customs to ask for a certain amount to be distributed amongst the officers through-but the whole Dominion. Whatever that amount may be, the officials of the department divide it up as best they can amongst those whom they think are deserving of it. The inspector reports to the commissioner tne efficiency of each officer, and the report is generally accepted by the minister. It has been not only my custom but that of my predecessor to follow that report closely. Of course, there are many cases where men are at their maximum for the positions which they hold, and they sometimes complain because they are not receiving increases when others are. For instance, if the hon. member will look over the list of salaries, he will find that landing waiters in Ontario and Quebec receive between $800 and $900 per annum; but that many of them have from $200 to $350 for overtime, so that they make very good salaries. These salaries are considered about the maximum in the eastern provinces. In the western provinces, the landing waiters are paid $100 or $150 more. When the landing waiters reach that salary, the increases do not come as fast as they do in the case of other officers. Therefore, when a landing waiter is receiving a salary of $900, he generally has it supplemented by $200 or $300 for overtime. The clerks are supposed to hold higher, positions and they receive higher salaries than the landjng waiters, but they do not receive overtime. I would like to see the outside service on the same basis as the inside so that no fault could be found. My officials and I have tried to divide up the salaries in such a way that

very little fault can be found in any way and especially so far as politics is concerned.
On what basis does the minister allow the extra amount for overtime? A man might be able to do his work without overtime.

The men are paid at the rate of thirty cents an hour for all their time over ten hours. They must get a certificate from the collector or the surveyor that the work has actually been performed. The surveyor in a large port like Montreal has charge of the outside work. In smaller ports, where there are only half a dozen officers, they may be working at a railway station or at a steamboat landing, and it is easy to have a check on work of that nature. An officer might have to be on duty all the time. In my own town, a ferry boat runs until twelve o'clock at night and an officer must be on duty until that time. The men divide up that time:	One man will be on
duty for a couple of hours and another for a . couple of hours each night. At a railway station they have to attend certain trains, such as express trains, coming in, and it is very easy for the collector to keep a check on the men's time. I do not think there would be much loss.
What is the estimate of the cost of collection of customs for the province of New Brunswick for the year 1914-15?

I have only the general
figures. I have not Nova Scotia separately.	,

Before preparing his
Estimates for 1915-16, did the minister go into the matter with his officers and make any effort to reduce them by say two million dollars or by one dollar?

My officials tell me that
they have as much work with the war now on as they had prior to the war; in fact, a great deal more work has been thrown on the Customs Department on account of the war. The men are all busy and they will use the whole vote of last year. With that information before me, I do not see how I would be justified in asking for a smaller vote than that of last year.
Then the minister has not endeavoured to reduce the Estimates?

Yes, I took the matter up
with the officials of my department and that is the information they gave me, and I must rely upon the officials who understand the situation thoroughly.

The minister has said
that on account of the war the work has been so heavy. I am curious to know how the war has increased the work of the customs officers seeing that the revenues have declined.

The war has made it necessary for us to have many more officers watching vessels coming in and going out. We have to watch the imports and exports much more closely because of the prohibitions made necessary by the war. Take it, for instance, at Bridgeburg, where many cars cross-we have to have officials there to watch very closely. The Commissioner of Customs tells me that the officials are busier than they have ever been though the revenue has decreased.
How many officers have been appointed in the Customs Department since the day when war was declared, the 4th of August?

As I said before dinner, we designed to make no new appointments at all. A number of our officers went to the war and their places have not been filled, the others being used as relieving officers until these men return. When vacancies occur, we do not fill them unless it is absolutely necessary. Therefore, the new appointments are practically nil.

Since that return we have
had 39 deaths, 16 superannuations, 43 dismissals and 45 resignations.

give me the figures since 1911?

Will the minister please state what are the duties of these special officers?

These officers are for special preventive service. When we receive complaints of smuggling or learn that smuggling is suspected, these officers are detailed to look up the case. Also they are supposed to travel around and learn if smuggling is going on. Such officers are needed throughout the Dominion. We have two 15i
or three in Nova Scotia, two in New Brunswick, two or more in Quebec, and so with the other provinces.

In some cases, I think thet
duty of these officers consists mainly in _ collecting their pay at the end of the months

Last session I called
attention to the lack of a customs officer at New Waterford. Has the hon. gentleman changed his mind since then, and does he intend to appoint a collector of customs there?
We have not decided. At present I am trying to keep down the expense as much as possible, and to avoid the appointment of more officers while the war is on.

I am sorry the hon. gentleman has not succeeded in keeping down the expense. We do not see much difference in the expenditure except that the estimate of expenditure for next year shows an increase. I do not think there is another town of the size of New Waterford in the whole Dominion of Canada without a customs officer. The minister may not know it, but this is a town of about 8,000 people. I do not know whether the minister or any one in his department has had any correspondence in regard to the matter, but I have had correspondence, both before I left Regina and since I came to the city of Ottawa, with regard to the question of establishing a port of entry at a little place called Overland.

r

I have had some correspondence with the Department of Customs extending over two years on the question of the importation of certain horses. The department wrote me some time ago that, as far as they are concerned, the question was closed. At the same time I do not think it will do any harm to state briefly the facts. A man named Underwood, a farmer not very far from where I live, imported nineteen horses from some portion of the United States. He purchased the horses and brought them into the country by means of certain certificates and seven of these certificates were discovered on investigation by the Customs Department to have been false certificates. The reason for holding an .investigation was that some of the horses were quarantined by a Govern-

ment veterinary in the West for dourine which caused an' investigation into where they came from and the discovery of the false certificates. I am not concerned with the vendor of the horses in the United States. Underwood brought the horses into Canada, he paid for them to the vendor in the United States and filed declarations with the department that, as far as he was concerned, he had acted in good faith. I believe that the purchaser of these horses did act in absolute good faith and why he should have been punished by the imposition of double duty on him I have never been able to make out. I have taken that up with the department for two years but ceased doing so when I was informed that the matter had been finally closed. I cannot help representing to the minister that this man suffered an injury which he did not deserve. He acted in good faith and should not have been charged $2,200 by way of double duty owing to the false certificates under which the horses were brought into Canada, he having no part in the fraud.
The horses were fraudulently imported into this country.
Not by this man.
The hon. member agrees that they came in fraudulently.
M do not so far as he was concerned.

The man referred to claims
that he had nothing to do with the fraud, but at the same time we follow the goods. We followed the horses in this case and held them as responsible for this duty. In cases of this kind these matters are always dealt with by the regular seizing officers of the staff, and in this case double duty was imposed. That is one of the smallest fines that is imposed on fraudulent importations, and we could not possibly let men off in such cases, because if we accepted such pleas as this man's, then in every case of fraudulent importation a similar claim would be made and we feel that in business of this kind if we find the importer is not really the guilty man we impose only double duty. In other cases we would take the whole goods, simply take the horses and dispose of them and fine him the penalty of tire total value. In this ease while he may think it is a hardship, I feel that he got off as reasonably as many others have in similar positions.

According to a
return brought down, up to March 10, 1914, there was a very large increase shown in the number of employees in the Interior Department, both in -the inside and the outside service. I have no doubt that since that date, owing to peculiar conditions existing in certain parts of the West, there has been a further increase, and as to a portion of that increase I have no criticism to offer. Up to March 10, 1914, the return showed 301 dismissals in the Department of the Interior and 1,649 new appointments. In certain parts of western Canada with which I am familiar, I believe that a large number of these new appointments were absolutely useless to the public service. I can give an instance of four homestead inspectors being employed by the present Government in the Dominion lands office in my own city, where there is not work for one. The late Government [DOT]for twelve or thirteen years only employed two homestead inspectors there and now I believe there are four, whereas any one who knows, the district knows that the homesteads are practically exhausted in that vicinity and one homestead inspector could easily do the work. I am sure the present Minister of the Interior does not want to waste the public money by keeping an unnecessary number of homestead inspectors sitting around doing nothing. A couple of years ago a man named Sipes -was employed as homestead inspector in the country tributary to Regina, and according to an answer given me by the Minister of the Interior some two years ago, for the four or five months that he was so employed he did not make a single homestead inspection. I know that the present Minister of the Interior has too much respect for his own reputation to waste, the public money in this way. The homestead office in Regina is just an instance of what is going on in other parts of Western Canada. The appointment of 1,649 new officials in the last three years is due to the fact that the present Government has largely increased the number of officials operating in the Department of the Interior in western Canada. Homestead work is decreasing, 'and immigration during the past eighteen months, even before the war,

as we all know, amounted to almost nothing, so that this enormous number of officials should not be needed. I do not wish to impute any motives to the present Minister of the Interior, but surely there must be some reason for keeping men in these various places in western Canada, doing practically nothing.

In addition to what the
Solicitor-General explained before recess, as to appointments to fill vacancies by resignations and deaths, etc., there is something further to be said. I understand that Professor Shortt used an expression in an address in the People's Forum on Sunday night, which was calculated to leave an entirely erroneous impression on the public mind. In my own department the appointments probably numbered twice the number of dismissals, but that included not only the appointees referred to by the Solicitor-General, but a very large number of temporary employees. For example, the office of the Surveyor-General employs a large number of men for six months in the year when their services are dispensed with, and next year there will be forty or fifty new men engaged who, while only temporary employees, are reckoned as new appointees by the Government. The Interior Department has nearly 900 employees, and up to last year we have had as many as 140 temporary employees engaged for six months in the year, as the Civil Service Act will not allow us to retain the services of these temporary employees for a longer period. Professor Shortt not having explained this situation, his remarks have left an erroneous impression on the public mind. In reference to the homestead inspectors, I understand that some of these gentlemen have been transferred to other districts. An additional reason why there have been more homestead inspectors appointed is that we have been trying to	afford greater convenience to the farmers of the country who enter for their lands, and who ordinarily would have to pay a good deal of money and spend a good deal of their time travelling long distances to the nearest subagency, for their patent, by instructing many of our homestead inspectors to visit those farmers on their farms. This is a great convenience to the farming community, and I have many requests from the settlers that it should be continued.

That was done
before.

Not nearly to the same extent as it has been done for the last eighteen months. It may be that there are more employees now in some of these offices than the work of the offices would warrant, but the hon. gentleman knows that in these hard times it is not very nice to dismiss employees, unless you have ground for it, and we do not wish to impose any undue hardships upon these men. No person has ever complained to me before with regard to the land office at Regina. I understand there are four officials in that office at present. It is true that there are not many homesteads remaining in that district, but at the same time there is considerable work in the office. The present land agent there has gone to the front and somebody had to take his place. At all events, I can assure my hon. friend from Regina that I certainly have not appointed as many officials as I have had demands for appointments.

this grant, if any, is being spent in connection with the Saskatchewan river and on what water-power?

I cannot give the facts in finite such detail as that. The whole expenditure is in the prairie provinces, particularly in Alberta and Saskatchewan-$2o 000 in Saskatchewan. nection with small water-powers, getting information for those who wish to develop them. much of this money is being spent in connection with the supposed diversion of the Saskatchewan river or the taking of water from that river. What has been done in
connection with that scheme? And is it the intention of the Government to actually take water from the Saskatchewan and distribute it in the surrounding country?

A delegation from Prince Albert made requests of the department on this subject about eighteen months ago. I remember that several gentlemen waited upon myself on my western tour in 1913. As a result of that delegation an investigation was authorized with a view to improving, if possible, the low water conditions in the river and placing the municipal plant of Prince Albert at Lacolle in a more satisfactory position for the production of power. The future of hydro-electric development along the Saskatchewan river is largely dependent on the storage facilities which may be available throughout the basin. The importance of this question to the industrial life of the prairie is such that it

must receive immediate and energetic attention. The great demand for cheap power throughout the West makes it necessary that every possible effort be put forth to secure the same, and the storage investigations now going on have in view the best methods of securing satisfactory results from hydro-electric development. This appropriation will enable us to carry on the investigation which we have been conducting during the past year.

Do I understand from the minister that this item of |17,000 has only to do with the matter of the investigation of the power contained in the Saskatchewan river? For the last few years requests have been made by the city of Prince Albert to the Government to grant them some assistance in respect of obtaining some assistance for the development of iLacolle Falls up to the present time,
I believe, without avail. I am scarcely able to gather from the minister, however, whether this $17,000, which includes all the money voted for the purpose of investigating water schemes along the Saskatchewan river, is to be devoted entirely to the development of Lacolle falls for the benefit of the city of Prince Albert, or whether it has anything to do with the distribution of water for domestic purposes to the people who reside south and east of the Saskatchewan river.

It is not at all confined to the particular item to which the hon. gentleman has referred. It is for surveys and investigations all along the Saskatchewan river, in what is known as the Saskatchewan basin.

I do not wish to be unduly persistent about this matter, but in the province in which I reside we have been led to beiieve that the Government had on foot a tremendous scheme having in view the supplying of pure water to the cities of Moosejaw and Regina and to the rural inhabitants of the adjoining country by diverting water from the Saskatchewan river and bringing it down through Buffalo lake to the southeastern part of the province. In a section of the country where water is scarcer than it is in the eastern provinces, it is important that steps be taken to secure an adequate supply of pure water. As I say, we have been led to believe that the Government has had this scheme in view, with the object of getting
rid of the question of the scarcity of water in the province of Saskatchewan for all time to come.
I may say that there is no provision in these Estimates for an expenditure such as the hon. gentleman has mentioned. We think it is not a suitable time to launch out on such an extensive enterprise.
Does the minister consider that it would not be a proper expenditure?
No, I say this is not the proper time to incur it.
I suppose it is the view of the minister that it is all right to spend the money somewhere else, but that it is not the proper time to spend the money there.

This item is very largely increased this year. It is an item that provides for examination and exploration, which examination and exploration can not be turned to actual account without a vast future expenditure of money. It seems to me that if we are in a condition of financial stringency which precludes the probability of any of these large expenditures being carried forward within a short time, these processes of examination and exploration might very well be slackened off for the present or for a year or two, instead of being increased as they have been. I do not wish to make the criticism in any factious spirit, but, having regard to prevailing conditions, and especially to the financial situation, I take the ground that this is an item which might very well be reduced at this session without throwing any discredit upon the general purposes that the Government has in view, and without affecting the ultimate carrying out of these objects. But, inasmuch as the giving effect to the results of these examinations or explorations must involve a vast expenditure of money, which money is not likely to be available, the preliminary expenditures might be postponed for the time being, or reduced rather than increased.

A special staff of engineers is engaged on this work. The hon. gentleman will realize the difficulties which would arise if we dismissed the staff and re-engaged later persons who possibly would not be so conversant with the work. Having set out to do this work, we thought it better to continue it, and we have kept the engineers together. This item covers not only the expenses of surveys, but several sub-items as well, such as: publishing reports in connection with investigations

and surveys; expenses of official administration at the head office; drainage and reclamation. There are several items under the one heading of water-powers. I realize that this is not a good year for launching out on new enterprises, and we have endeavoured not to do that, but in respect of this enterprise which we have already undertaken, we thought it would be more economical to continue it, especially in view of the fact that we have a special staff engaged for the purpose.

May I ask the minister whether he has had any complaints or protests in respect to the extension of the boundaries of Waterloo Lakes Park?

I think I have had one or two complaints in regard to the extension.
I cannot remember from whom, but I think the matter has been brought to my attention.

Is it proposed to reduce the size of that park? I understand that there has been some fric-10 p.m. tion, in the matter between the Forestry Department and the Parks Department. The matter is quite important, in a way; I am sure that some petitions have been sent in by stockmen and settlers.
The matter is unaer consideration. I think I can tell the hon. gentleman that it is most likely that there will be a redaction in the size of the park.
In what particular feature is the very considerable reduction in this item?

In nearly all the parks we are having a reduction of expenditure. There was a large expenditure in connection with the Banff park last year in build-
ing the bath house. That is now completed and will effect quite a saving.

Is any money being
made out of the Wainwright buffalo park? What are you doing with the surplus buffalo? They are breeding very rapidly.

I do not think there is
much money being made out of the park, there may be some but not very much.
Is there any intention of increasing the area of the Jasper park? At present there is a stretch of, I think, ten miles on each side of the railway.

If my memory serves me
correctly it was enlarged a year or two ago.

Before leaving Edmonton, I was spoken to in reference to a suggestion that the area should be increased very considerably. There was some objection to any very considerable increase, the idea was that it was fair and reasonable to have a stretch of say from ten to twenty miles on" each side of the railway itrack under the special park regulations. I wish to put myself on record as in favour of not having an unreasonable extension of the park regulations.

Has the minister had
any representations from the residents of Wainwright asking for the removal of the buffalo park?
Not that I am aware of.

I understand a petition was sent in asking the Government to remove that park, that they required the land for arable purposes. Wainwright is the centre of a good arable country and it is considered a detriment to have the whole southern section of the district occupied by a buffalo park.
I was under the impression that the people of Wainwright originally were all in favour of having it there.
At one time, yes.
It may be that they have changed their minds and sent in some petition, but I cannot recall it.

At Jasper park the Government have made very considerable expenditures in road-making and otherwise. They have added greatly to the advantages of the park as a point for tourists and pleasure seekers but they have been so very particular in their determination that

everything be kept up to the highest standard that, up to the present time, time, no accommodation has been provided for visitors at the park. The natural beauty is there, but of course unless a visitor is able to obtain food and shelter, the scenery is not of any serious advantage to him, and he passes on through. I understand it is the intention of the Government to require the erection of very first-class hotel accommodation in the park. I would suggest that in these hard times the minister lower the standard required by his officials and endeavour to secure moderate accommodation which will meet the immediate purposes of the tourist trade and enable the visitors of to-day to enjoy the scenery and advantages of the park. There are two important points. Jasper is what might be called the capital of the park, and Poco-hontas the point at which people leave to go into the hot springs. There should be accomodation for travellers at both.
Engraving, lithographing, printing and preparation of maps, plans and kindred publications of the Dominion, including necessary materials for same, $81,500.

This increase is offset by the reduction which we have made in the surveys, so that there is no real increase in the vote, and it is caused by the establishment of a blue print plant in connection with the department for lithographing, etc.

Homestead maps of the West are issued showing the progress of settlement from year to year. They are unique, and most valuable to any one who desires to follow them. They are gotten up in four separate sheets, one Manitoba, one Saskatchewan, one of the southern part of Alberta and one of the northern part of Alberta. I suppose that owing to the great amount of labour involved, in making corrections from year to year, the staff is occupied nearly the whole year, so that the last of the four maps gets out only at the end of the year. That is to say, the map of Northern Alberta which gives the condition of settlement up to the beginning of 1914, does not reach the public until the end of 1914. As the area covered by the map of Northern Alberta includes the Peace River country, which today is attracting attention and settlement more than any other section of the West, I would suggest to the minister that this map be made the first care of his staff in getting out these four maps.

I recognize the force of
my hon. friend's remarks. As homesteaders are flocking into the Peace River District at the present time I think we might be justified in giving that map the first claim, although my hon. friend no doubt remembers the argument that is sometimes made against the department for encouraging settlers to go up into the north country in advance of transportation facilities. The settlers there frequently become a charge on the department for grub-staking and so on. After they have raised their crops they say: We have no transportation facilities; you encouraged us by your immigration literature to locate here, and now you must look after us. That must be taken into consideration, although personally I do not think that a map would induce people to settle there; but undoubtedly it would be a great source of information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have practically to take the two departments together. Last year we had 178 officials in the Marine Department; this year we have 143, or 35 less. In the Naval Department last year we had 84 officials, and we have now 125, or 41 more. In explanation I may say that under the statute the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is also the Minister of Naval Service. The two departments are under the one minister, and for the purpose of equalizing the work of those departments we have found it desirable to transfer a considerable quantity of

work from the Marine and Fisheries Department to the Naval Service Department. This ' equalizes the work and promotes greater efficiency. For the Naval Service Department, which deals not merely with naval affairs, but with fisheries protection, the hydrographic and tidal surveys, and other branches of some importance, had a far less share of work than the Marine-and Fisheries Department. By the changes we have made, 38 clerks are transferred from the Marine Department to the Naval Service Department, which accounts for the great diminution in the number of marine officials, and the great increase in the number of JIaval Service officials. There are no salary increases in the Marine Department except the ordinary statutory increases. There are apparently three extra clerks, but when it comes to be looked into one of them is the naval architect, who has been employed by the department for many years. He has always been in the outside service, but it is now proposed to place him in the inside service on the same footing as other Civil Service officials. The other two extra clerks are stenographers at $500 a year. In the Naval Service Department too, there are apparently three extra clerks, but they are all outside service, officials who are being transferred to the inside ' service. There are no promotions, and no increases except the statutory increases.

Can the minister explain why there has been no return from the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Naval Service as to the number of officials appointed or dismissed ? A return was moved for more than a year ago asking for these figu"es in regard to all departments, and apparently the Post Office Department and the Marine and Fisheries Department are the only ones that have not complied with that order. Can the minister tell us how many officials have been dismissed and how many appointed since this Government took office ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not able to say offhand, but speaking from memory I do not think a single official in the insiae service of either the Marine and Fisheries Department or the Naval Service Department has been dismissed since the Government took office.

I understand that most of the changes have taken place in the outside service. Might I suggest, to the 
minister that his department follow the good example of the other departments and furnish the House with that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know why it has not been done. I shall certainly have the information brought down.
There is apparently an increase in the total.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
For 1915-16 the total
salaries for	the two	departments	are$379,700, and	last year	$359,950.	In	thetwo there is an apparent increase of $20,000, but fully half of that is accounted for by the statutory increases, which in the case of most of the officials is $100 a year, although some of the lower ones get only $50. In addition to that, there is the salary of Mr! Duguid, the naval architect, who has been transferred from the outside to the inside service. That accounts for $4,000. Two	stenographers at	$500	ayear brings that'	up to	$5,000.
In addition, there is an inspector in the radio-telegraph branch at $1,600, an engineer in connection with the fish hatchery work, $1,800, and a clerk in the accountant's branch of the Naval Department, $500. These three officers were in the outside service, and they were transferred to the inside service. These items amount to $9,000 or $10,000, and the balance of the other $10,000 is represented by the statutory increases in the salaries of the officers.

Would the minister
furnish us with a complete list of the appointed and dismissed officials before he goes into the main estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will if it has not already been brought down.
A large number of offi-. cers were appointed in October as inspectors of pickled fish and fish canneries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The administration of that Act was handed over to us by the Agriculture Department and we re-appointed the officers, but it entailed no extra salaries.

Would it not be
better to appoint competent men and pay them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Perhaps it would.
Civil Government-Department of Naval Service, $220,600.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was done with the intention of equalizing the work of the departments. -Ever since there has been a Naval Department it has had to do with the administration of a portion of the fisheries, such as the fishery protection service and
other branches, and it was thought desirable to equalize the distribution of the work between the officials. The change was made in the public interest and it has worked well. The book referred to was published first of all in 1913 for distribution at the Toronto Exhibition where the Department for the first time made an exhibition of the fisheries wealth of Canada. There was an edition of 60,000 originally published and that soon ran out, and we are getting further demands from all parts of Canada. Our French citizens have been asking ior copies of this book so that we have had a translation made for distribution amongst them. I am glad my hon. friend from Guysborough approves of the book, and coming as he does from a fishing county he no doubt recognizes the value of fish as a food.

Why not say that it is issued by the Department of Marine and Fisheries?
!Mr. HAZEN : Because it is not issued by the Department of Marine and Fisheries; it is issued by the Department of Naval Affairs which has under its charge fishery matters. What difference does it make? I think it is better to speak the truth.
It makes a great difference. It is throwing ridicule upon the Department of Naval Service to say that this cookery book is issued by that department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No one has tried before to throw ridicule upon it.
I think the minister should not bring out another edition of this book and credit it to the Department of Naval Service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Then we would not be crediting it to the right department.

The Government will forgive the minister if- he is not quite frank in stating the name of the department issuing the book. I think he should state the fisheries branch.
Ocean and river service, $1,256,900.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I just want this item of the main estimates called. I am not calling it for the purpose of discussion.

The hon. minister will remember the plaims that are filed in his department with regard to the Behring sea fisheries. I do not know exactly which item they come under, and I presume they are not to this discussion; but I have received

several inquiries from men who laid claims before Judge Audette when he was going throughout the country and they are naturally anxious to know what progress is being made in regard to the matter. Perhaps while the minister is dealing with the estimates, ihe will be able to tell us in what state those claims are at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There have been a great many of those claims, and Judge Audette has investigated nearly all of them. He is going to Britisn Columbia in a very short time to dispose of the remaining ones in which he has not yet heard the evidence. That will wind up the hearing of the claims, and I understand he hopes to be able to make*a report dealing with the whole question some time- during the coming summer. The matter is getting to the point where it will be wound up very soon.
Progress reported.
